title: Presentation and diagonal of an affine action quotient stack
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $G$ be a smooth affine group scheme of finite type over $k$, and let $G$ act on an affine finite-type $k$-scheme $U=\operatorname{Spec}E$. Form $\mathcal X=[U/G]$ and $\pi:U\to\mathcal X$ as in [def-sfb-affine-action-quotient-stack]. Then $\mathcal X$ is a finite-type algebraic stack with affine diagonal, and $\pi$ is a smooth surjective atlas. Algebraic stack has the meaning in [def-sfb-algebraic-moduli-stack]; finite type is tested on scheme atlases using [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. The pullback of its diagonal along $U\times_kU\to\mathcal X\times_k\mathcal X$ is $(a,\operatorname{pr}_2):G\times_kU\to U\times_kU$. If every geometric stabilizer group scheme has dimension zero, this diagonal is quasi-finite and separated; quasi-finite here means finite type with finite geometric fibres, tested on scheme charts. For every algebraic space $T/k$, pullback by $\pi$ identifies maps $\mathcal X\to T$ with invariant maps $U\to T$, where invariance is equality after $a$ and $\operatorname{pr}_2$. For every algebraically closed extension $\Omega/k$, the map $U(\Omega)\to\mathcal X(\Omega)$ induces a bijection $U(\Omega)/G(\Omega)\simeq\pi_0(\mathcal X(\Omega))$, where $\pi_0$ denotes isomorphism classes of objects. The invariant ring is the equalizer $E^G=\{e:\rho(e)=e\otimes1\}$ for the coordinate coaction $\rho:E\to E\otimes_k k[G]$. There is a canonical map $\phi:\mathcal X\to Y=\operatorname{Spec}(E^G)$ whose composite with $\pi$ is induced by $E^G\hookrightarrow E$. These assertions apply to $G=\operatorname{PGL}_{r,k}$ for every $r\geq1$: this group scheme is smooth, affine and of finite type over any field. Here the geometric stabilizer at $v\in U(\Omega)$ is the closed subgroup scheme $G_v$ of $G_\Omega$ defined by $g\cdot v=v$; dimension is topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Algebraically closed uses [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Affineness of the diagonal means its pullback by every affine scheme is an affine scheme; separatedness of the diagonal means its own diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. The coaction is written in the order $E\otimes_k k[G]$ by swapping the factors in the pullback of $a$.

proof.text: Put $R=G\times_kU$, with source $s(g,u)=u$, target $t(g,u)=g\cdot u$, identity $(1,u)$, inverse $(g,u)\mapsto(g^{-1},g\cdot u)$ and composition $((h,g\cdot u),(g,u))\mapsto(hg,u)$. The action identities give every groupoid identity on test-scheme points. The projection $s$ is a base change of the smooth $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, hence is smooth by the chartwise calculus. The displayed involution interchanges $s$ and $t$, so $t$ is smooth too. Thus this is a smooth scheme groupoid. All maps are over $k$.

source.place: definition-quotient-stack (Tag 044Q), action groupoid, with explicit groupoid operations

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-groupoid-fppf-quotient] with $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$, object scheme $U$ and arrow space the scheme $R=G\times_kU$ and the torsor-comparison theorem to this left action. The latter identifies the resulting stack with precisely the fibred groupoid $\mathcal X$ of the statement and identifies its object map with $\pi$. Consequently $\mathcal X$ is algebraic and $\pi$ is smooth and surjective. In fact the base change of $\pi$ by an object $(P,f)$ over $T$ is the scheme $P$: a point $p$ gives $x=f(p)$ and the trivialization $G_T\to P$, $h\mapsto hp$, and any such trivialization is determined by the image of $1$. This verifies scheme representability of the atlas in the torsor convention. Since the scheme atlas $U$ is finite type over $k$, $\mathcal X$ is finite type under the atlas convention stipulated in the item; the required finite-type atlas is $U$ itself.

The cited quotient theorem identifies $R$ with $U\times_{\mathcal X}U$ by $r\mapsto(s(r),t(r),i(r))$. Swap the two objects and invert the specified arrow in this 2-fibre product; this is an involutive isomorphism, so the same relation has projection $(t,s)=(a,\operatorname{pr}_2)$ to $U\times_kU$. This gives the claimed pullback of the diagonal in the target/source convention. Write $H=k[G]$. Both its source and target are affine, with rings $H\otimes_kE$ and $E\otimes_kE$. The source ring is generated over $k$ by finitely many generators of $H$ and of $E$, so these same elements generate it over $E\otimes_kE$ via the map in question. This proves finite type of $(t,s)$; it is affine. It is separated: the multiplication map $B\otimes_A B\to B$ for any ring map $A\to B$ is surjective, as $b$ is the image of $b\otimes1$, so the relative diagonal of $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is a closed immersion. Here apply this to the two displayed rings. The product stack is algebraic: descent is componentwise, for two objects over any test scheme $T$, its isomorphism space is the fibre product over $T$ of their two component isomorphism spaces, an algebraic space by the categorical fibre-product assertion of [lem-trf-space-fibre-products-etale-covers], and the product atlas is smooth surjective. Indeed $\pi\times\pi$ is smooth surjective by factoring it into two base changes of $\pi$ and composing. The locality theorem therefore descends affineness, finite type and separatedness from $(t,s)$ to $\Delta_{\mathcal X/k}$. This proves the affine diagonal assertion and, already without any stabilizer assumption, its separatedness.

proof.text: Fix an algebraically closed extension $\Omega/k$ and an object $\xi=(P,f)$ of $\mathcal X(\Omega)$. By step 2 its scheme $P$ is the base change of the smooth surjective atlas. The current calculus identifies surjectivity with the chart test and with lifting after field extension. Applied to $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, it gives a point of $P$ after a field extension, so $P$ is nonempty. Smooth base change makes $P$ smooth over $\Omega$, hence locally of finite type. Choose a nonempty affine neighbourhood small enough that its coordinate algebra is finitely generated over $\Omega$. The closed-point lemma supplies a closed point of this affine scheme (affine schemes are qcqs and hence spectral by the two cited theorems; sobriety makes them Kolmogorov, since two points with the same closure would be two generic points of one irreducible closed subset), and clause 1 of the affine Nullstellensatz identifies its residue field with $\Omega$. It gives $p\in P(\Omega)$. The torsor trivialization $h\mapsto hp$ identifies $\xi$ with $\pi(f(p))$. Thus $U(\Omega)\to\pi_0(\mathcal X(\Omega))$ is surjective. Notice that no assertion about torsors over fields that are not algebraically closed was used.

proof.text: For $x,y\in U(\Omega)$ the arrows between their atlas objects are the $g\in G(\Omega)$ with $g\cdot x=y$, by the action groupoid and the presentation/comparison theorems. In the left-torsor convention the corresponding torsor isomorphism is right multiplication by $g^{-1}$, as in the comparison statement. Thus two atlas objects are isomorphic exactly when their points are in the same $G(\Omega)$-orbit. Combined with step 4 this proves the stated orbit/isomorphism-class bijection.

source.place: Tag 04WM, explicit functor on arrows; spaces-groupoids.tex Tag 04M9

proof.text: Now assume every geometric stabilizer has dimension zero. For a geometric point $(x,y)\in(U\times_kU)(\Omega)$ the fibre $F$ of $(a,\operatorname{pr}_2)$ is the transporter $\{g\in G_\Omega:g\cdot y=x\}$. It is an affine scheme of finite type over $\Omega$: its coordinate ring is the base change to $\Omega$ of the finite-type algebra in step 3. If it is nonempty, the affine qcqs and spectral theorems give quasi-compactness and the Kolmogorov property (by uniqueness of generic points); the closed-point lemma and clause 1 of the affine Nullstellensatz give $g_0\in F(\Omega)$. The maps $G_y\to F$, $h\mapsto g_0h$, and $F\to G_y$, $g\mapsto g_0^{-1}g$, are inverse scheme maps: the equations $hy=y$ and $gy=x$ verify the factorizations on every test scheme, and the inverse identities are the group laws. Thus $F$ has dimension zero. It is Noetherian by finite type over the Noetherian scheme $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ (a one-point scheme with field local ring). The zero-dimensional Noetherian finiteness theorem now gives finite underlying space. Empty fibres are finite as well. This argument concerns the whole stabilizer scheme, including possible nilpotents, not just its group of geometric points.

proof.text: Step 3 gave finite type and separatedness of the chart map $(a,\operatorname{pr}_2)$, and step 6 gave finite geometric fibres under the stabilizer assumption. Hence that chart map is quasi-finite in the stated finite-type/finite-geometric-fibre convention. Set $q=\pi\times\pi:U\times_kU\to\mathcal X\times_k\mathcal X$. As in step 3, $q$ factors into two base changes of the representable smooth surjective atlas $\pi$; the chartwise calculus makes $q$ smooth and surjective, hence flat and locally of finite presentation. Its current surjectivity equivalence ensures that after every scheme base change every surjective etale scheme chart maps surjectively to the base, exactly the cover condition used here. Its source is a scheme, in particular an algebraic space, and its target is algebraic by step 3. The diagonal is representable by algebraic spaces by the presentation theorem, and its pullback by $q$ is exactly the chart map computed in step 3. Thus all hypotheses of the fppf locality theorem hold for this diagonal and this cover. Its quasi-finite and separated clauses prove that $\Delta_{\mathcal X/k}$ is quasi-finite and separated.

source.place: Tag 04XD for quasi-finite and separated; spaces-descent.tex Tags 0427 and 0421

proof.text: Let $T/k$ be any algebraic space. Restriction of a map $\mathcal X\to T$ to $U$ is invariant, since the action groupoid arrows map to identity arrows in the discrete groupoid of $T$. Conversely let $b:U\to T$ satisfy $ba=b\operatorname{pr}_2$. On an object $(P,f)$ over a scheme $S$, choose an fppf trivializing cover $S_i\to S$ and its sections $p_i$. On overlaps $p_j=g_{ij}p_i$ for a unique $g_{ij}\in G(S_i\times_SS_j)$, so $bf(p_j)=bf(p_i)$ by invariance and equivariance. Since $T$ is an fppf sheaf by its definition, these maps glue uniquely to a map $S\to T$. Two choices give the same answer after their common refinement and hence before refinement. For a base map or a torsor isomorphism the maps agree on a trivializing cover, so sheaf uniqueness gives functoriality. This defines a map $\mathcal X\to T$. It restricts to $b$ on trivial torsors. Any other extension has these same local values on every object and therefore agrees on every object and arrow. This proves the asserted identification, including uniqueness, with no separatedness assumption on $T$.

source.place: Tag 044U, elementary torsor/sheaf expansion of the coequalizer assertion; examples-stacks.tex Tag 04WM

proof.text: The pullbacks of functions along $a$ and $\operatorname{pr}_2$ are $\rho$ and $e\mapsto e\otimes1$ in the chosen tensor-factor order. Their equalizer is a $k$-subalgebra of $E$, because both maps preserve addition, multiplication, scalars and $1$; it is exactly the ring denoted $E^G$ in the statement. By contravariance of affine spectra the inclusion $E^G\hookrightarrow E$ induces $q:U\to\operatorname{Spec}(E^G)$. The equality $\rho(e)=e\otimes1$ for $e\in E^G$ says exactly that $qa=q\operatorname{pr}_2$. The affine scheme $Y=\operatorname{Spec}(E^G)$ is an algebraic space over $k$: its functor of points on $k$-schemes is an fppf sheaf, since every fppf covering is an fpqc covering [lem-trf-fppf-covering-is-fpqc] and morphisms into a scheme that agree on overlaps glue uniquely along an fpqc covering [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent], the glued map being over $k$ by uniqueness; its diagonal is representable because the fibre product of two maps $h_T\to h_Y$ is represented by the scheme fibre product $T\times_YT'$ [def-pc-fibre-product]; and $\mathrm{id}_Y$ is a surjective etale atlas. Step 8, with $T=Y$, gives a unique map $\phi:\mathcal X\to T$ with $\phi\pi=q$, hence the canonical map claimed. No finite-generation assertion for $E^G$ is needed here.

proof.text: For $r\geq1$, the existing PGL structure theorem states that $\operatorname{PGL}_{r,k}$ is smooth, affine and of finite type over $k$. These are exactly the group hypotheses used in steps 1--9, so all conclusions apply to any affine finite-type scheme on which it acts. For $r=1$ it is the trivial group scheme, which is explicitly covered by that theorem; no assumption on the characteristic or on the invertibility of $r$ is imposed.
